title: How hard could implementing DTLS 1.3 possibly be?
excerpt: The lore of how Pion got DTLS 1.3, and DTLS explained with interactive demos you can play with!
content_html:
In January 2026, I somehow ended up leading Pion's DTLS 1.3 implementation and building most of it. It was still mostly an idea at that point, and I didn't really know how DTLS 1.3 worked. Most of the people who ended up building it with me didn't either :)

Ten months and ~400 commits later, DTLS 1.3 is the default in pion/dtls:

  • a one-round-trip handshake
  • post-quantum key exchange
  • Connection IDs, so your connection survives your phone switching networks
  • 0-RTT resumption
  • Encrypted Client Hello

I wanted to write down the lore of how this happened, and also explain DTLS the way I wish someone had explained it to me. So this is both, with interactive demos you can poke and break along the way.

  • Clientwants to talk to the server, privately

  • Serverwants to know it is really talking to the client

  • Mallorysits on the wire, reads everything, changes what she can

Backstory and lore

If you don't want to read the backstory, skip to the implementation.

Pion's Plans for DTLS 1.3 issue had been open since February 2020, when the spec was still a draft. It became RFC 9147 in 2022, but nobody had the time it takes to actually commit to it, and every so often someone asked for updates...

Meanwhile, in January 2025, Sean DuBois, who created Pion and its libraries, told me (a nobody) I could co-maintain it with him and handed me owner access to the whole thing. Sean trusted me more than I trusted me :)

I created Pion's Discord server, reviewed PRs every day, contributed new features across the stack, and talked my friends into contributing. But I kept opening that DTLS 1.3 issue, staring at it, and closing the tab. For DTLS fixes and reviews were fine, but anything bigger felt like I'd create an RCE!

Then, in May 2025, Theo (Theodor Signebøen Midtlien) said in the issue that he'd applied to NLnet. The same day, Sean offered to review and merge everything, and to go knock on companies' doors for money if NLnet said no. NLnet said yes, and Theo announced the grant on August 6.

At the time, R Chiu and I were spending a lot of time in Pion's SCTP stack, the thing WebRTC data channels run on. She implemented RACK loss recovery.

Adriano Sela Aviles had also joined while working with us on Pion's TURN implementation, and sent really important PRs, but he and R had their own lives and were not able to go all the way with the implementation.

I'd read the spec once and was comfortable with it from a high-level POV, so I was excited to help with reviews. R Chiu helped with the key schedule. But it was Theo's project, and while we wanted to help, we didn't want to get in the way.

People were waiting for it. In December, just as the project was starting, Justin Uberti from OpenAI, where Sean had worked, asked for updates. They wanted "reduced RTTs during connection setup, and also … post-quantum crypto support." Lower RTTs meant you didn't have to wait as long for voice AI to start.

Theo put together a high-level MVP plan and opened skeleton PRs, but then life got busy, including a new job at NetBird! By January 2026, I was starting a new WebRTC job at Upwork, but I don't have a family yet, so I have free time after work :) Theo was happy to hand me the project. I promised we'd do his plan right and extend it, including the parts outside the WebRTC subset. I wanted a real DTLS 1.3 library that Pion also happens to use, because users outside WebRTC need resumption, 0-RTT and Connection IDs too.

I don't want to get paid for my work on Pion, because I don't want to treat it as a job. I also wanted people to build it with me. So I asked my friends who had already contributed to Pion, Jade Kolos, Júlia Borges Paschoalinoto and Julia-Elena Roman, and later Jan Muška, to join the NLnet-funded effort, and recommended them to Theo. Then DTLS 1.3 was ours to finish :)

We had DTLS 1.2 extension parsers that didn't really understand DTLS 1.3, and an unmerged state machine skeleton. No record layer, no key schedule, no encryption, nothing that could finish a DTLS 1.3 handshake. And none of us had a real TLS background.

Reading TLS, and being too anxious to write it

Roughly four months passed between the handoff and our first record-layer implementation. There were extension and helper commits, but the main implementation was stalled. We kept reading specs and other implementations: RFC 9147, RFC 8446, RFC 9146, IETF write-ups. I was still mostly anxious: I wanted to do this right and didn't want to break stuff people were already using.

Then Sean asked how it was going. That's when we got his backing to really go ahead. He helped with the code design (where DTLS 1.3 would fit with 1.2 in a clean way), the FSM, Go idioms, cleaning up some old code, and later most of the DTLS 1.3 ACK reliability.

But most importantly, other than the technical parts, he made me confident enough to build it and break stuff along the way. He told me I could merge stuff without review!

We didn't have to understand every last thing before starting. He reviewed, merged, unblocked and encouraged. Without him, I think this would've taken another year or more.

Finally, a handshake

On May 13 we started the record layer. On June 19 we finally merged the state machine.

On July 7 I closed the six-year-old issue with this very reasonable estimate:

I think we'll have a working production ready MVP within two weeks.

That wasn't accurate.

The server's Finished verified on July 12, and on July 29 the client's Finished verified too. A Pion client and server finally completed a DTLS 1.3 handshake. On August 5 I got the first confirmation of DTLS 1.3 working in WebRTC against Chrome! I hadn't slept for two days, and couldn't believe it. I'd written most of it without testing against another implementation lol.

Our team's write-up has a line I really like: "Finished" is a different story. The handshake was just the beginning. August was more than a hundred commits: Connection IDs, KeyUpdate, HelloRetryRequest, SRTP negotiation, rewriting extension parsing, and a week deleting duplicated code that I badly underestimated.

We tagged the first v4 release candidate on September 26. Two days later I closed the tracking issue, and DTLS 1.3 went into Pion WebRTC's next major version. People outside WebRTC were already trying it on real IoT clusters. Seeing them pick up resumption and the other features motivated me to finish ECH and 0-RTT.

On October 14 I said support was complete. Before we released it, Anthropic rolled out their OSS scanner, and we sent pion/dtls through it. It found many old issues, but also new ones in the new implementation. Yey, we got to fix them before release!

On October 31, DTLS 1.3 became the default in pion/dtls. No more "not implemented" errors, examples using 1.3 by default, and 1.2 one option away. v4.0.0-rc.8 is tagged, final v4 is next, and Pion WebRTC's next major version will bring it to everyone who uses it.

So enough with the yapping! Let's dive in. But before we get into DTLS, what even is the D in DTLS? And how does it relate to TLS?

Phone calls and postcards

Everything on the internet travels in packets. What happens when one goes missing depends on how you're sending them.

TCP is a phone call. You get a connection, and everything you say arrives complete and in order, or not at all. If a packet gets lost on the way, TCP notices, sends it again, and makes everything after it wait until it arrives. You never see the gap, the conversation just pauses.

UDP is postcards. Each packet, a datagram, travels on its own with its own address, and it either arrives whole or not at all. Postcards get lost, arrive out of order, and sometimes the same one shows up twice. Nobody resends anything and nobody waits.

Here are both, carrying the same message, with the same bad luck:

Try it a few times and tap a packet or two in flight. TCP always delivers a perfect HELLO, PION!, but it can take longer to finish, because one lost letter holds up every letter behind it. This is called head-of-line blocking (and it's the boogeyman of the real-time world). UDP finishes sooner, but what arrives is a mess. The app can sort it if it numbered its postcards, but the lost ones are just gone.

The mess is fine for a lot of things, because for real-time media late is the same as lost. One can argue that an audio packet that arrives 300ms late is useless: the moment it was meant for has already passed. Video is even worse: a frame is usually split into many packets, and later frames depend on earlier ones, so waiting for one lost packet holds up everything behind it, the same head-of-line blocking as TCP. It's better to keep going and decide what's actually worth recovering.

WebRTC, for example, has a few ways to do that on top of UDP. RTP numbers every packet, like the postcards above, so the receiver knows exactly what's missing. With NACK, it tells the sender which sequence numbers it lost and the sender resends just those. That costs at least one extra round trip, so when there's no time to wait there's FEC (forward error correction): the sender adds a few extra parity packets, and the receiver rebuilds a lost packet from them without asking for anything. There's a whole post about FEC in Pion if you want the details.

That's why WebRTC tries(*) to send its media and data over UDP: it gets to decide what's worth waiting for.

(*) WebRTC can also use TCP transports, either directly with ICE-TCP or through a relay with TURN over TCP or TLS. DTLS is still used in both: with ICE-TCP the DTLS records are carried inside the TCP stream, and with TURN only the hop to the relay is TCP, and the relay usually forwards the same DTLS packets to the other side over UDP.

Anyway, the problem is that the protocol that keeps the internet private, TLS, was designed for phone calls. It assumes nothing gets lost, reordered or duplicated. Put it on postcards and it falls apart.

DTLS (Datagram TLS) is TLS rebuilt for postcards. To see what had to change, we first need to know what TLS actually promises.

What TLS promises

TLS makes three promises about the conversation between Client and Server:

  1. Nobody else can read it. (Confidentiality.)
  2. Nobody can change it without getting caught. (Integrity.)
  3. You're talking to who you think you're talking to. (Authentication.)

Mallory is the reason all three exist. She sits on the wire, which in real life is your coffee shop's Wi-Fi, a compromised router, a shady ISP, or anyone else between you and the server. Every packet goes through her.

You might think encryption takes care of the second one too. If Mallory can't read the message, how is she going to change it into anything useful? Try it:

Encryption alone hides what you said, but a stream cipher like AES-CTR just XORs your message with a keystream, so flipping a bit in the ciphertext flips the same bit in the plaintext. Mallory doesn't need the key, she only needs to know where 10 is in the message.

That's why every cipher in TLS 1.3 and DTLS 1.3 is an AEAD (authenticated encryption with associated data). AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 encrypt the record and compute a tag over it. Change one bit anywhere and the tag doesn't match, so the record gets dropped. Older TLS versions did encryption and authentication separately and got burned by the gaps between them more than once, so TLS 1.3 removed every cipher that isn't an AEAD.

Agreeing on a key in front of Mallory

AEADs need a key that only Client and Server know. But they've never met before, and every message between them goes through Mallory, so they have to agree on a secret while she listens to every word. We can explain it with paint:

Each side keeps a secret and only sends a mix. Mallory sees both mixes but can't un-mix them, so both sides end up with the same final color and she can't make it herself. In real crypto the "paint" is elliptic-curve math (X25519 is the common one), and "un-mixing" means solving a problem no current computer can solve in any reasonable time.

In TLS 1.3 the client doesn't wait to be asked. It guesses which key exchange the server will accept and puts its half, the key_share, in the very first message, the ClientHello. If the guess is right, the server answers with its own half and can start encrypting right away. That's why TLS 1.3 needs one round trip where TLS 1.2 needed two.

Key exchange alone doesn't stop Mallory from sitting in the middle and doing a separate key exchange with each side. That's what promise three is for. The server proves who it is by signing the handshake with its certificate's private key (the CertificateVerify message). Then both sides send a Finished message, a MAC over every handshake message so far (the transcript). If Mallory changed even one byte anywhere in the handshake, the transcripts won't match and the checks fail. Be Mallory and try:

Watch what catches her each time. If she touches the hellos, the transcripts stop matching, so the server's signature and the Finished MACs fail. If she swaps the key shares, she gets surprisingly far, until the server has to prove who it is. She can fake a key exchange, but she can't sign as server.example without its private key, and no CA will vouch for her own certificate. Well, unless she finds a CA whose private key is literally 4, which actually happened this October :)

That's how it works on the web, for example, where a CA says which certificate belongs to server.example. Standard WebRTC peers don't use CAs for authentication. Instead, each peer has its own certificate (which can be generated on the spot and self-signed) and puts its fingerprint, a SHA-256 hash of that certificate, in the SDP (Session Description Protocol) it sends through your signaling server:

a=fingerprint:sha-256 4A:AD:B9:B1:3F:82:18:3B:54:02:12:DF:3E:5D:49:6B:...

After the DTLS handshake, each side hashes the certificate the other side actually used and compares it with the fingerprint from the SDP, which is usually sent over HTTPS or a WebSocket over TLS. If Mallory swaps in her own certificate, the hash won't match and the connection fails. In WebRTC both sides send a certificate, so both sides get checked. The catch is that DTLS is only as trustworthy as your signaling: if Mallory can edit the SDP, she can put her own fingerprint in it.

Some connections don't use certificates at all. With a pre-shared key (PSK), both sides already share a secret, for example a key that was put on an IoT device at the factory, and knowing the key is the proof of identity. The handshake keys come from the PSK, so without it Mallory can't finish the handshake as either side. It's a lot cheaper than certificates, which is why it's popular on small devices. More on PSKs later.

So that's TLS in four steps:

  1. hello with a key share
  2. hello back with a key share
  3. encrypted proof of identity
  4. Finished

Now let's put it on postcards.

Why TLS falls apart on postcards

TLS assumes it's on a phone call, so it takes some shortcuts, and every one of them breaks on UDP.

It counts silently. Every TLS record is encrypted with a nonce derived from a sequence number, but the number is never sent, both sides just count 0, 1, 2... On a phone call that's safe. With postcards, one lost record means the receiver thinks record 5 is record 4, uses the wrong nonce, and every record after that fails to decrypt. Drop one record and watch:

One lost postcard and the TLS receiver is off by one forever. So DTLS puts the epoch and sequence number in every record header, in the clear. (DTLS 1.3 encrypts them again, more on that later.)

It assumes the handshake arrives. In TLS a lost handshake message is TCP's problem, in DTLS it's yours. Each side groups its handshake messages into flights and starts a retransmission timer. If the next flight from the other side doesn't show up in time, it sends its own flight again.

It assumes any message fits. A TLS handshake message can be up to 16 MB and TCP will happily stream it. A UDP datagram that's too big for the path gets dropped, or chopped into IP fragments that plenty of firewalls and NATs drop anyway, and the safe size on the internet is about 1200 bytes give or take, while a certificate chain is often several kilobytes. So DTLS adds a 12-byte header to every handshake message that says which message it is, how long the whole thing is, and which bytes this fragment carries:

This one actually bit us. A retransmitted message is allowed to be fragmented differently from the original. OvenMediaEngine, an OpenSSL-based media server, splits its handshakes into tiny 256-byte fragments, and Pion's DTLS 1.2 reassembly assumed fragment boundaries would line up, so after a single lost datagram the handshake could never finish. Tristan Matthews fixed it by making reassembly track which bytes it has instead of which fragments.

Post-quantum crypto makes it worse. The post-quantum key share Pion sends by default is 1216 bytes on its own, so now even the first message of the handshake doesn't fit in one datagram.

And of course that broke something. wolfSSL, which a lot of embedded devices run, wants the first ClientHello in a single datagram so it can answer without keeping any state, and by default it just won't take a fragmented one. Most people using pion/dtls directly are doing IoT, so that's the worst place to break. Raising the MTU doesn't help either, the ClientHello needs 1415 bytes and plenty of networks can't do that. So now Pion sends an X25519 share next to the hybrid one like Go does, and clients put plain X25519 first so the first ClientHello fits again. If the server wants post-quantum, it asks for it with a HelloRetryRequest, so we still get ML-KEM everywhere it's supported. Clients with early data keep ML-KEM first, because a retry throws the early data away. I kinda get the X25519MLKEM768 hate now :(

It assumes nobody repeats things. Networks do occasionally duplicate packets, but TCP throws away bytes it already has, and if Mallory spliced an old record into the stream, TLS's silent counter would have moved on and it wouldn't decrypt. DTLS just put the sequence number in the header, so with UDP Mallory can record a perfectly valid encrypted packet and send it again as many times as she wants, and it decrypts fine because it is valid. So DTLS keeps a sliding replay window, a bitmap of recently seen sequence numbers, and drops anything it already saw or that's too old to tell:

Now switch to "slide, then authenticate" and have Mallory send her garbage. One fake record with a huge sequence number pushes the window a million packets ahead, and every real packet after it looks ancient. That's why the window should only move after a record is authenticated.

It assumes the sender's address is real. TCP's handshake proves the other side can receive packets at its address before anything else happens. UDP has nothing like that, so Mallory can write anyone's address on her postcards. If she sends a small ClientHello with a victim's address, the server answers the victim with its big first flight, certificates and all, turning a few hundred bytes into a few kilobytes aimed at someone else. So DTLS servers answer a new ClientHello with a small cookie first, and only do real work after the client echoes the cookie back, proving it can receive mail at that address:

In WebRTC, ICE's connectivity checks often prove the address before DTLS even starts, so is the cookie still worth a round trip? Not always: SFUs usually run ICE-lite, which only answers checks and never sends its own, so the server never learns whether the client's address is real. Philipp Hancke and I are working on a more nuanced default.

That's the "D": explicit sequence numbers, timers, fragments, a replay window and cookies, all added to TLS so it survives postcards. DTLS 1.2 already did all of this, and Pion had supported it for years.

DTLS 1.3 starts from TLS 1.3 and redesigns a lot of this. Let's go through the pieces.

Talking to both DTLS versions

My first big design decision was that a connection is always in exactly one of three modes. I wanted to make this super explicit because of a Firefox bug that broke calls to Pion: Firefox speaks both versions, and its fallback to 1.2 went wrong. We kept coming back to this for the rest of the year:

  1. DTLS 1.2 only.
  2. DTLS 1.3 only.
  3. Dual, where the version isn't decided yet and the client must still be able to talk to an old 1.2-only server. In this mode we're also explicit about which state we're in:
    1. Not decided yet.
    2. Decided to continue with 1.3.
    3. Decided to downgrade to 1.2.

A lot of our hardest bugs were in that third one. Pick a client and a server and connect:

Dual mode is tricky. The client sends one ClientHello that has to be a valid DTLS 1.2 hello and a valid DTLS 1.3 hello at the same time, and it only finds out which one it was when the server answers. If the answer is 1.2, everything from the 1.3 attempt has to disappear without a trace. Our first fallback didn't clean everything up. You can switch that bug on in the demo above. And Mallory can't force a downgrade either: a 1.3 server that gets pushed down to 1.2 writes DOWNGRD at the end of its random value, and the client notices.

The record layer

A DTLS 1.2 record header is 13 bytes, on every single packet. For a video call that's a lot of bytes spent on bookkeeping. DTLS 1.3 replaced it with a unified header, where the first byte is a set of flags that say what comes after it. Poke the bits:

Three things changed.

It's smaller. The smallest DTLS 1.3 header is 2 bytes. The content type (handshake, alert, application data) isn't in the header anymore, it moved inside the encryption, so Mallory can't even tell what kind of record she's looking at.

The sequence number is encrypted. DTLS had to put the sequence number on every postcard, but that's also a tracking number for Mallory: she can count packets, follow a connection across networks, and measure exactly how much was sent. DTLS 1.3 encrypts those bits with a mask derived from the record's own ciphertext. Toggle "what Mallory sees" and click next a few times: the real numbers go 42, 43, 44, and she just sees noise.

It's mostly implicit. Only the low 8 or 16 bits of the sequence number and the low 2 bits of the epoch are sent, and the receiver reconstructs the rest from what it expects next. That only works because the receiver keeps careful state about every epoch, which brings us to keys.

Where keys come from

As I wrote in the team's write-up: the names are scarier than the concepts. HKDF, AEAD, transcript hash, epoch, each is a small idea with a scary name.

TLS 1.3 doesn't use a key, it uses a whole family of keys, each derived from the one before it and each protecting a different part of the conversation. Encrypted handshake messages get one key, application data gets another, and after a KeyUpdate you get a fresh one and the old one can be forgotten. In DTLS each of these keys lives in its own epoch, and the epoch number in the header tells the receiver which key to use.

The thing that produces them is the key schedule, and it's built from one tool: HKDF, which takes some secret material and stretches it into as many independent keys as you need. You can try the actual key schedule here. It's computed in your browser:

Click "new handshake" and watch every value below it change. One fresh key exchange at the top, and every key below it is new and unrelated to any previous connection. This is called forward secrecy: if someone steals the server's certificate key next year, they still can't decrypt today's call, because the keys never depended on it.

The other input is the transcript hash, a running hash of every handshake message so far. Mixing it into the keys means that if Mallory changed anything, the two sides derive different keys and just can't talk. I spent a good part of June getting that transcript exactly right. Miss one byte, hash a message twice, or accidentally include a retransmission, and nothing works. And nothing tells you why it didn't :)

Ciphers and post-quantum key exchange

In July we implemented the ciphers (AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305), record number masks, seal and open. On July 1 Pion also got X25519MLKEM768, the hybrid post-quantum key exchange. It does an X25519 exchange and an ML-KEM exchange together, so the result is safe as long as either one holds up. This matters because of harvest now, decrypt later: someone recording your encrypted call today could decrypt it in fifteen years with a big enough quantum computer, unless the key exchange already resists one. By August it was on by default.

Not everyone is a fan of ML-KEM, though. Daniel J. Bernstein, the person behind X25519 and ChaCha20, campaigned against an IETF draft that uses ML-KEM on its own in TLS, and says the NSA is paying to get it standardized. He calls the hybrid, the one Pion uses, "much more sensible". If ML-KEM ever falls, X25519 is still there :)

Flights and ACKs

Reliability in DTLS 1.2 is pretty basic. Nobody acknowledges anything: if I don't hear back in time, I resend my entire flight, even if only one packet out of six was lost. And if the reply was lost instead, the other side resends its entire flight too.

DTLS 1.3 added an ACK message: "here are exactly the records I got." The sender resends only the gaps, and the receiver can send an ACK as soon as it notices a hole, without waiting for a timer. Same bad luck on both sides:

After "Finished", it really was a different story: there's a whole second state machine for session tickets and KeyUpdate, with its own ACKs and retransmissions. So getting Finished to work still leaves you with basically another protocol to implement :(

Connection IDs and changing networks

In WebRTC, calls can use ICE to find a new path when the network changes (Pion has a post about that), so they don't need Connection IDs, but they matter for IoT users.

Without a Connection ID, a DTLS server finds the connection a packet belongs to by where it came from: the client's IP address and port. Now walk out of your house. Your phone drops Wi-Fi, switches to cellular and gets a new address, and the server has never heard of it.

With a Connection ID, every record carries a short ID that the server picked, and the server finds the connection by ID instead of by address, so your connection survives the walk to the car. Pion already had CIDs for DTLS 1.2. In 1.3 they're part of the core protocol and really different, so we had to rebuild them into the new record layer, while reworking the DTLS 1.2 implementation so we wouldn't have duplicated code.

Of course Mallory can make this a problem too. If the server just follows the newest address a valid record came from, she can record one real packet and resend it with the victim's address on it, and the server redirects the whole video stream at someone who never asked for it. The specs saw this coming: CIDs in both DTLS 1.2 and 1.3 already said you must check that a new address can receive before switching to it, but never said how, so many implementation didn't enforce this (including Pion's DTLS 1.2).

Return Routability Check (RFC 9853) is the standard way: before trusting a new address, send it a small challenge, and only switch once the answer comes back. Try the second half of the demo with RRC off, then on.

RRC has a fun backstory. While reading the IETF shepherd write-up for the RRC draft, I found this: "We have two different clients (Eclipse/Californium & Pion) that interoperate with a server." Someone had used a Pion fork for testing! I got so excited about that, I went and built a real production RRC for upstream Pion while we were still doing DTLS 1.3, instead of postponing it until after the release!

Resumption, 0-RTT, and Encrypted Client Hello

Pre-shared keys and resumption. If the client and server talked before, or share a key from somewhere else, they can skip the certificate work entirely. Smaller handshakes, less CPU, and still forward secret when combined with a fresh key exchange.

0-RTT. If you talked before, you don't have to wait at all. With a resumed session, the client can send application data in its very first flight, encrypted with keys from last time. Here's how the handshakes compare, and the catch:

0-RTT data can be replayed. There's no fresh input from the server protecting it yet, so Mallory can capture it and send it again. That's fine for "show me the menu", not fine for "pay $10", so applications have to opt in and only send things that are safe to repeat. It also gives up some forward secrecy: go back to the key schedule, turn on "with PSK" and press "new handshake" a few times. The early secret never changes, because it only comes from the PSK, so anyone who steals that PSK later can decrypt the early data.

Encrypted Client Hello. TLS 1.3 already encrypts the certificate, so which site you visit is hidden, except for one field: the ClientHello carries the server's name (the SNI) in plain text, because the server needs it to pick the right certificate. ECH encrypts the real ClientHello inside an outer one that only names a generic front server:

While implementing ECH, I wanted our implementation to match crypto/tls, because I felt it was the right thing to do. But as soon as I started, I found two places where Go's own crypto/tls was too lenient with ECH configurations, and sent them patches (one, two). So we went back to doing it our own way, which turned out to be the stricter implementation.

Testing the implementation

I think setting up interop tests was the best decision we made all year. Testing Pion against itself only proves both sides share the same assumptions, so in April I created pion/dtls-interop and froze releases from main until interop was ready. It tests Pion against:

  • OpenSSL 3 and 4
  • BoringSSL
  • wolfSSL
  • Mbed TLS
  • the TLS-Anvil conformance suite
  • Pion's own v3

On September 28, when DTLS 1.3 went into Pion WebRTC's next major version, I added it to pion/browser-tests, which runs Pion WebRTC against Chrome, Firefox, Edge and Safari.

The report before release

Anthropic's OSS scanner went through pion/dtls and sent us a report. On October 16 I opened #1228, "Fix all issues reported by anthropics/oss-scanner", and spent the busiest two weeks of the whole project working through it. Most of the real issues were in DTLS 1.2, session resumption and shared code that had been in production for years, not the new DTLS 1.3 code, and we fixed them on both main and the v3 branch so existing users can upgrade without changing anything. After spending so much time anxious about breaking stuff, that felt really good :)

sirzooro independently reported a few of the same issues (and others), found with Claude Opus 5.5.

Why exporting connection state is tricky

There was one finding we couldn't fix in code.

Pion v3 lets you export a connection's state and resume it later, for example to hand a connection from one process to another. The scanner pointed out that nothing stops both the original and the restored connection from continuing to send. Both would keep encrypting with the same AES-GCM key and the same sequence numbers, and the nonce is built from the sequence number.

Reusing a nonce with AES-GCM is one of the worst things you can do in cryptography. Here's why:

AES-GCM encrypts by XORing your message with a keystream generated from the key and the nonce. Same key and nonce means same keystream, so XORing the two ciphertexts cancels the keystream out and leaves the two plaintexts XORed together. Mallory doesn't need the key: she guesses a likely word in one message, and the other message shows up around it. The same reuse also leaks enough for her to forge tags.

Sadly we couldn't make the v3 API safe without breaking everyone who uses it, so v3 now documents loudly that a restored state must be used exactly once. In v4, Resume requires ExportState, which closes the original connection as part of the export, so there's no way to keep using both.

Thank you

I'm really happy with what we built. I never thought I'd lead a project this big all the way to the end, and that still feels a bit weird. But the part I'm most proud of is the people. Whenever I got stuck, or talked about a problem for hours in our Discord server or group chats, someone was always there to listen and help.

None of this would exist without the people I built it with: Sean DuBois, Theodor Signebøen Midtlien, Adriano Sela Aviles, R Chiu, Jade Kolos, Júlia Borges Paschoalinoto, Julia-Elena Roman and Jan Muška. Thank you for all the reviews and testing, and sorry for how annoying I was about stuff I found cool :)

Huge thanks to Thomas Legris. He runs DTLS for a very large fleet of IoT devices with Pion on the server side, and at that scale every allocation per connection gets multiplied by hundreds of thousands. One of his PRs starts with "At scale (700k connections) - I detected some heavy allocations, especially at handshake." Over the year he sent a lot of optimizations:

  • fewer copies and allocations in the handshake
  • pre-allocated buffers for marshalling
  • pooled timers
  • a reworked PacketConn with fewer goroutines per connection, in pion/dtls and pion/transport
  • a fix for a connection leak

Then he ran the release candidates in production, and they worked without a single problem.

Resumption got tested before it was even tagged, and I can't tell you how happy that made me :) ybaldus opened an issue about deadlines while building SWIM on pion/dtls, which "requires short lived connections and session resumption to be scalable." When I said resumption wasn't tagged yet: "Don't mind tagging it yet I can also use the current master commit." The report turned into a fix that applies read and write deadlines to the handshake.

Leonard (ltlobaro) did the same from the IoT side, where "DTLS 1.2 handshakes easily take up most of the device traffic". They played with the DTLS 1.3 resumption example, found that key logging didn't work with DTLS 1.3, and it was fixed in rc.5 the same day.

devArnoud ran DTLS 1.3 against a cellular modem whose TLS stack is wolfSSL baked into its firmware, and every handshake failed. When the server asked the modem to send its ClientHello again, wolfSSL sent the same extensions in a different order. The spec doesn't strictly allow that, but for compatibility Pion accepts it now.

enobufs tried DTLS 1.3 with WebRTC early and helped with the keying-material exporter.

Thanks to Philipp Hancke for testing DTLS 1.3 in his SPED implementation, which embeds the DTLS handshake in STUN, and for noticing that Pion sent a session ticket even to clients that never use resumption.

Thank you to everyone who reviewed, tested, reported and fixed things along the way. Thanks to NLnet and the NGI0 Commons Fund for funding work like this, and to the Anthropic OSS scanner team for the report that made v4 safer before anyone found out the hard way.

And thank you for reading this far :) Now go break something.

Come chat with us on the Pion Discord about anything.

P.S. Everything went perfectly except one silly mistake: I forgot to wire the message hooks into DTLS 1.3 after refactoring the handshake messages, and one hook was left taking a 1.2-only type, so we had to break the API in v4.0.1, our very first patch a few minutes later after we tagged v4 :(
content_text: In January 2026, I somehow ended up leading Pion's DTLS 1.3 implementation and building most of it. It was still mostly an idea at that point, and I didn't really know how DTLS 1.3 worked. Most of the people who ended up building it with me didn't either :)Ten months and ~400 commits later, DTLS 1.3 is the default in pion/dtls:a one-round-trip handshakepost-quantum key exchangeConnection IDs, so your connection survives your phone switching networks0-RTT resumptionEncrypted Client HelloI wanted to write down the lore of how this happened, and also explain DTLS the way I wish someone had explained it to me. So this is both, with interactive demos you can poke and break along the way.Clientwants to talk to the server, privatelyServerwants to know it is really talking to the clientMallorysits on the wire, reads everything, changes what she canBackstory and loreIf you don't want to read the backstory, skip to the implementation.Pion's Plans for DTLS 1.3 issue had been open since February 2020, when the spec was still a draft. It became RFC 9147 in 2022, but nobody had the time it takes to actually commit to it, and every so often someone asked for updates...Meanwhile, in January 2025, Sean DuBois, who created Pion and its libraries, told me (a nobody) I could co-maintain it with him and handed me owner access to the whole thing. Sean trusted me more than I trusted me :)I created Pion's Discord server, reviewed PRs every day, contributed new features across the stack, and talked my friends into contributing. But I kept opening that DTLS 1.3 issue, staring at it, and closing the tab. For DTLS fixes and reviews were fine, but anything bigger felt like I'd create an RCE!Then, in May 2025, Theo (Theodor Signebøen Midtlien) said in the issue that he'd applied to NLnet. The same day, Sean offered to review and merge everything, and to go knock on companies' doors for money if NLnet said no. NLnet said yes, and Theo announced the grant on August 6.At the time, R Chiu and I were spending a lot of time in Pion's SCTP stack, the thing WebRTC data channels run on. She implemented RACK loss recovery.Adriano Sela Aviles had also joined while working with us on Pion's TURN implementation, and sent really important PRs, but he and R had their own lives and were not able to go all the way with the implementation.I'd read the spec once and was comfortable with it from a high-level POV, so I was excited to help with reviews. R Chiu helped with the key schedule. But it was Theo's project, and while we wanted to help, we didn't want to get in the way.People were waiting for it. In December, just as the project was starting, Justin Uberti from OpenAI, where Sean had worked, asked for updates. They wanted "reduced RTTs during connection setup, and also … post-quantum crypto support." Lower RTTs meant you didn't have to wait as long for voice AI to start.Theo put together a high-level MVP plan and opened skeleton PRs, but then life got busy, including a new job at NetBird! By January 2026, I was starting a new WebRTC job at Upwork, but I don't have a family yet, so I have free time after work :) Theo was happy to hand me the project. I promised we'd do his plan right and extend it, including the parts outside the WebRTC subset. I wanted a real DTLS 1.3 library that Pion also happens to use, because users outside WebRTC need resumption, 0-RTT and Connection IDs too.I don't want to get paid for my work on Pion, because I don't want to treat it as a job. I also wanted people to build it with me. So I asked my friends who had already contributed to Pion, Jade Kolos, Júlia Borges Paschoalinoto and Julia-Elena Roman, and later Jan Muška, to join the NLnet-funded effort, and recommended them to Theo. Then DTLS 1.3 was ours to finish :)We had DTLS 1.2 extension parsers that didn't really understand DTLS 1.3, and an unmerged state machine skeleton. No record layer, no key schedule, no encryption, nothing that could finish a DTLS 1.3 handshake. And none of us had a real TLS background.Reading TLS, and being too anxious to write itRoughly four months passed between the handoff and our first record-layer implementation. There were extension and helper commits, but the main implementation was stalled. We kept reading specs and other implementations: RFC 9147, RFC 8446, RFC 9146, IETF write-ups. I was still mostly anxious: I wanted to do this right and didn't want to break stuff people were already using.Then Sean asked how it was going. That's when we got his backing to really go ahead. He helped with the code design (where DTLS 1.3 would fit with 1.2 in a clean way), the FSM, Go idioms, cleaning up some old code, and later most of the DTLS 1.3 ACK reliability.But most importantly, other than the technical parts, he made me confident enough to build it and break stuff along the way. He told me I could merge stuff without review!We didn't have to understand every last thing before starting. He reviewed, merged, unblocked and encouraged. Without him, I think this would've taken another year or more.Finally, a handshakeOn May 13 we started the record layer. On June 19 we finally merged the state machine.On July 7 I closed the six-year-old issue with this very reasonable estimate:I think we'll have a working production ready MVP within two weeks.That wasn't accurate.The server's Finished verified on July 12, and on July 29 the client's Finished verified too. A Pion client and server finally completed a DTLS 1.3 handshake. On August 5 I got the first confirmation of DTLS 1.3 working in WebRTC against Chrome! I hadn't slept for two days, and couldn't believe it. I'd written most of it without testing against another implementation lol.Our team's write-up has a line I really like: "Finished" is a different story. The handshake was just the beginning. August was more than a hundred commits: Connection IDs, KeyUpdate, HelloRetryRequest, SRTP negotiation, rewriting extension parsing, and a week deleting duplicated code that I badly underestimated.We tagged the first v4 release candidate on September 26. Two days later I closed the tracking issue, and DTLS 1.3 went into Pion WebRTC's next major version. People outside WebRTC were already trying it on real IoT clusters. Seeing them pick up resumption and the other features motivated me to finish ECH and 0-RTT.On October 14 I said support was complete. Before we released it, Anthropic rolled out their OSS scanner, and we sent pion/dtls through it. It found many old issues, but also new ones in the new implementation. Yey, we got to fix them before release!On October 31, DTLS 1.3 became the default in pion/dtls. No more "not implemented" errors, examples using 1.3 by default, and 1.2 one option away. v4.0.0-rc.8 is tagged, final v4 is next, and Pion WebRTC's next major version will bring it to everyone who uses it.So enough with the yapping! Let's dive in. But before we get into DTLS, what even is the D in DTLS? And how does it relate to TLS?Phone calls and postcardsEverything on the internet travels in packets. What happens when one goes missing depends on how you're sending them.TCP is a phone call. You get a connection, and everything you say arrives complete and in order, or not at all. If a packet gets lost on the way, TCP notices, sends it again, and makes everything after it wait until it arrives. You never see the gap, the conversation just pauses.UDP is postcards. Each packet, a datagram, travels on its own with its own address, and it either arrives whole or not at all. Postcards get lost, arrive out of order, and sometimes the same one shows up twice. Nobody resends anything and nobody waits.Here are both, carrying the same message, with the same bad luck: loss 15% jitter 40%TCPa phone callapp seeswaiting for you to press sendUDPpostcardsapp seeswaiting for you to press send Tap a packet in flight to drop it. TCP holds back everything after a gap until the missing packet is resent. UDP hands over whatever shows up, in whatever order it shows up. If the app numbers its postcards, it can sort them afterwards, but it can't fill the gaps. Try it a few times and tap a packet or two in flight. TCP always delivers a perfect HELLO, PION!, but it can take longer to finish, because one lost letter holds up every letter behind it. This is called head-of-line blocking (and it's the boogeyman of the real-time world). UDP finishes sooner, but what arrives is a mess. The app can sort it if it numbered its postcards, but the lost ones are just gone.The mess is fine for a lot of things, because for real-time media late is the same as lost. One can argue that an audio packet that arrives 300ms late is useless: the moment it was meant for has already passed. Video is even worse: a frame is usually split into many packets, and later frames depend on earlier ones, so waiting for one lost packet holds up everything behind it, the same head-of-line blocking as TCP. It's better to keep going and decide what's actually worth recovering.WebRTC, for example, has a few ways to do that on top of UDP. RTP numbers every packet, like the postcards above, so the receiver knows exactly what's missing. With NACK, it tells the sender which sequence numbers it lost and the sender resends just those. That costs at least one extra round trip, so when there's no time to wait there's FEC (forward error correction): the sender adds a few extra parity packets, and the receiver rebuilds a lost packet from them without asking for anything. There's a whole post about FEC in Pion if you want the details.That's why WebRTC tries(*) to send its media and data over UDP: it gets to decide what's worth waiting for.(*) WebRTC can also use TCP transports, either directly with ICE-TCP or through a relay with TURN over TCP or TLS. DTLS is still used in both: with ICE-TCP the DTLS records are carried inside the TCP stream, and with TURN only the hop to the relay is TCP, and the relay usually forwards the same DTLS packets to the other side over UDP.Anyway, the problem is that the protocol that keeps the internet private, TLS, was designed for phone calls. It assumes nothing gets lost, reordered or duplicated. Put it on postcards and it falls apart.DTLS (Datagram TLS) is TLS rebuilt for postcards. To see what had to change, we first need to know what TLS actually promises.What TLS promisesTLS makes three promises about the conversation between Client and Server:Nobody else can read it. (Confidentiality.)Nobody can change it without getting caught. (Integrity.)You're talking to who you think you're talking to. (Authentication.)Mallory is the reason all three exist. She sits on the wire, which in real life is your coffee shop's Wi-Fi, a compromised router, a shady ISP, or anyone else between you and the server. Every packet goes through her.You might think encryption takes care of the second one too. If Mallory can't read the message, how is she going to change it into anything useful? Try it: on the wire (what Mallory sees)50415920424f4220243130 as text: PAY BOB $10server got…waiting for the packet Have Mallory read the packet, then change it, on each tab. With AES-CTR she can’t read a thing, yet she still rewrites the amount. Only AES-GCM’s tag catches her. Encryption alone hides what you said, but a stream cipher like AES-CTR just XORs your message with a keystream, so flipping a bit in the ciphertext flips the same bit in the plaintext. Mallory doesn't need the key, she only needs to know where 10 is in the message.That's why every cipher in TLS 1.3 and DTLS 1.3 is an AEAD (authenticated encryption with associated data). AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 encrypt the record and compute a tag over it. Change one bit anywhere and the tag doesn't match, so the record gets dropped. Older TLS versions did encryption and authentication separately and got burned by the gaps between them more than once, so TLS 1.3 removed every cipher that isn't an AEAD.Agreeing on a key in front of MalloryAEADs need a key that only Client and Server know. But they've never met before, and every message between them goes through Mallory, so they have to agree on a secret while she listens to every word. We can explain it with paint:1. a common paint, public2. a secret paint each, never sent?3. mix and send it over the wire+ = →←+ = 4. mix what arrived with your own secret+ = #835c5a+ = #997151+ = #835c5a✓ Client and Server match: yellow + red + blue, one part each.✗ Mallory is off: her mix has two parts yellow, and paint doesn’t un-mix. Pick a secret paint for each side. Their final colors always match; Mallory’s never does. In TLS 1.3 this happens in the very first message (the key_share in ClientHello), which is why the handshake takes one round trip. Pion’s DTLS 1.3 actually defaults to X25519MLKEM768, which adds a post-quantum exchange on top. Each side keeps a secret and only sends a mix. Mallory sees both mixes but can't un-mix them, so both sides end up with the same final color and she can't make it herself. In real crypto the "paint" is elliptic-curve math (X25519 is the common one), and "un-mixing" means solving a problem no current computer can solve in any reasonable time.In TLS 1.3 the client doesn't wait to be asked. It guesses which key exchange the server will accept and puts its half, the key_share, in the very first message, the ClientHello. If the guess is right, the server answers with its own half and can start encrypting right away. That's why TLS 1.3 needs one round trip where TLS 1.2 needed two.Key exchange alone doesn't stop Mallory from sitting in the middle and doing a separate key exchange with each side. That's what promise three is for. The server proves who it is by signing the handshake with its certificate's private key (the CertificateVerify message). Then both sides send a Finished message, a MAC over every handshake message so far (the transcript). If Mallory changed even one byte anywhere in the handshake, the transcripts won't match and the checks fail. Be Mallory and try:attack the handshakeClientMallory, on the wireI’ll just watch.Server Pick Mallory’s move, then run the handshake. Pick a move for Mallory and run the handshake. Each attack slips past some checks, never all of them. The crypto is real (SHA-256 transcripts, ECDSA P-256 signatures, HMAC Finished, X25519 keys), but messages are hashed as text fields rather than wire bytes, and the certificate is a toy: one CA signature over a name and a key. Watch what catches her each time. If she touches the hellos, the transcripts stop matching, so the server's signature and the Finished MACs fail. If she swaps the key shares, she gets surprisingly far, until the server has to prove who it is. She can fake a key exchange, but she can't sign as server.example without its private key, and no CA will vouch for her own certificate. Well, unless she finds a CA whose private key is literally 4, which actually happened this October :)That's how it works on the web, for example, where a CA says which certificate belongs to server.example. Standard WebRTC peers don't use CAs for authentication. Instead, each peer has its own certificate (which can be generated on the spot and self-signed) and puts its fingerprint, a SHA-256 hash of that certificate, in the SDP (Session Description Protocol) it sends through your signaling server:a=fingerprint:sha-256 4A:AD:B9:B1:3F:82:18:3B:54:02:12:DF:3E:5D:49:6B:...After the DTLS handshake, each side hashes the certificate the other side actually used and compares it with the fingerprint from the SDP, which is usually sent over HTTPS or a WebSocket over TLS. If Mallory swaps in her own certificate, the hash won't match and the connection fails. In WebRTC both sides send a certificate, so both sides get checked. The catch is that DTLS is only as trustworthy as your signaling: if Mallory can edit the SDP, she can put her own fingerprint in it.Some connections don't use certificates at all. With a pre-shared key (PSK), both sides already share a secret, for example a key that was put on an IoT device at the factory, and knowing the key is the proof of identity. The handshake keys come from the PSK, so without it Mallory can't finish the handshake as either side. It's a lot cheaper than certificates, which is why it's popular on small devices. More on PSKs later.So that's TLS in four steps:hello with a key sharehello back with a key shareencrypted proof of identityFinishedNow let's put it on postcards.Why TLS falls apart on postcardsTLS assumes it's on a phone call, so it takes some shortcuts, and every one of them breaks on UDP.It counts silently. Every TLS record is encrypted with a nonce derived from a sequence number, but the number is never sent, both sides just count 0, 1, 2... On a phone call that's safe. With postcards, one lost record means the receiver thinks record 5 is record 4, uses the wrong nonce, and every record after that fails to decrypt. Drop one record and watch:the counter nobody sends shuffle order TLS on UDPimplicit counter expects record 0server readsnonce = IV ⊕ record number. The number itself is never sent.waiting for you to press sendDTLSexplicit sequence numberreads seq from headerserver readsSame nonce, but the record number rides in the header, in the clear.waiting for you to press send Press send, then tap one record early on (or press lose one) to drop it. The same records fly in both lanes. TLS never learns a record went missing, so it opens every later one with the wrong nonce. Real TLS would hang up at the first ✗. DTLS reads the number off the header and just carries on. One lost postcard and the TLS receiver is off by one forever. So DTLS puts the epoch and sequence number in every record header, in the clear. (DTLS 1.3 encrypts them again, more on that later.)It assumes the handshake arrives. In TLS a lost handshake message is TCP's problem, in DTLS it's yours. Each side groups its handshake messages into flights and starts a retransmission timer. If the next flight from the other side doesn't show up in time, it sends its own flight again.It assumes any message fits. A TLS handshake message can be up to 16 MB and TCP will happily stream it. A UDP datagram that's too big for the path gets dropped, or chopped into IP fragments that plenty of firewalls and NATs drop anyway, and the safe size on the internet is about 1200 bytes give or take, while a certificate chain is often several kilobytes. So DTLS adds a 12-byte header to every handshake message that says which message it is, how long the whole thing is, and which bytes this fragment carries: MTU 1200ClientHello · 1,538 B · 2 fragments of up to 1,175 B cut to fit MTU 1200server's reassembly buffer01537 headers: 2 × (12 B handshake + 13 B record) = 50 B extra. TLS sends it in one piece with a 4 B header. Tap fragments on the wire to drop them, then retransmit only the missing bytes. Try changing the MTU before you do: the receiver doesn't care how the gap gets filled. (DTLS 1.2 just resends the whole flight on a timer. ACKs fix that, later.) This one actually bit us. A retransmitted message is allowed to be fragmented differently from the original. OvenMediaEngine, an OpenSSL-based media server, splits its handshakes into tiny 256-byte fragments, and Pion's DTLS 1.2 reassembly assumed fragment boundaries would line up, so after a single lost datagram the handshake could never finish. Tristan Matthews fixed it by making reassembly track which bytes it has instead of which fragments.Post-quantum crypto makes it worse. The post-quantum key share Pion sends by default is 1216 bytes on its own, so now even the first message of the handshake doesn't fit in one datagram.And of course that broke something. wolfSSL, which a lot of embedded devices run, wants the first ClientHello in a single datagram so it can answer without keeping any state, and by default it just won't take a fragmented one. Most people using pion/dtls directly are doing IoT, so that's the worst place to break. Raising the MTU doesn't help either, the ClientHello needs 1415 bytes and plenty of networks can't do that. So now Pion sends an X25519 share next to the hybrid one like Go does, and clients put plain X25519 first so the first ClientHello fits again. If the server wants post-quantum, it asks for it with a HelloRetryRequest, so we still get ML-KEM everywhere it's supported. Clients with early data keep ML-KEM first, because a retry throws the early data away. I kinda get the X25519MLKEM768 hate now :(It assumes nobody repeats things. Networks do occasionally duplicate packets, but TCP throws away bytes it already has, and if Mallory spliced an old record into the stream, TLS's silent counter would have moved on and it wouldn't decrypt. DTLS just put the sequence number in the header, so with UDP Mallory can record a perfectly valid encrypted packet and send it again as many times as she wants, and it decrypts fine because it is valid. So DTLS keeps a sliding replay window, a bitmap of recently seen sequence numbers, and drops anything it already saw or that's too old to tell:Mallory:too oldwindow 16–47new164711111111 11111111 11111111 10110111nothing received yet Real DTLS keeps 64 slots. It only slides the window for records that pass authentication, so forged junk can't push it forward. Green slots are sequence numbers already received. Tap any slot to deliver that number, or let Mallory replay things. Then switch to “slide, then authenticate” and send Mallory's garbage. Now switch to "slide, then authenticate" and have Mallory send her garbage. One fake record with a huge sequence number pushes the window a million packets ahead, and every real packet after it looks ancient. That's why the window should only move after a record is authenticated.It assumes the sender's address is real. TCP's handshake proves the other side can receive packets at its address before anything else happens. UDP has nothing like that, so Mallory can write anyone's address on her postcards. If she sends a small ClientHello with a victim's address, the server answers the victim with its big first flight, certificates and all, turning a few hundred bytes into a few kilobytes aimed at someone else. So DTLS servers answer a new ClientHello with a small cookie first, and only do real work after the client echoes the cookie back, proving it can receive mail at that address:MalloryClientHello · 200 Bfrom 203.0.113.7 (spoofed)servervictim203.0.113.7ServerHello + certificates… · 3,600 BMallory sent0 Bvictim got0 Bamplification–server state0 held server memory: half-open handshakes 0 Spoof a few ClientHellos with cookies off and watch what lands on the victim. Then turn cookies on and try again. WebRTC already checks the peer with ICE/STUN before DTLS starts, which is why Pion's WebRTC stack skips HelloVerifyRequest by default. In WebRTC, ICE's connectivity checks often prove the address before DTLS even starts, so is the cookie still worth a round trip? Not always: SFUs usually run ICE-lite, which only answers checks and never sends its own, so the server never learns whether the client's address is real. Philipp Hancke and I are working on a more nuanced default.That's the "D": explicit sequence numbers, timers, fragments, a replay window and cookies, all added to TLS so it survives postcards. DTLS 1.2 already did all of this, and Pion had supported it for years.DTLS 1.3 starts from TLS 1.3 and redesigns a lot of this. Let's go through the pieces.Talking to both DTLS versionsMy first big design decision was that a connection is always in exactly one of three modes. I wanted to make this super explicit because of a Firefox bug that broke calls to Pion: Firefox speaks both versions, and its fallback to 1.2 went wrong. We kept coming back to this for the rest of the year:DTLS 1.2 only.DTLS 1.3 only.Dual, where the version isn't decided yet and the client must still be able to talk to an old 1.2-only server. In this mode we're also explicit about which state we're in: Not decided yet.Decided to continue with 1.3.Decided to downgrade to 1.2.A lot of our hardest bugs were in that third one. The fallback bug is a simplified reconstruction of the one fixed in pion/dtls#1030, where the 1.2 fallback dropped 1.2 extensions or offered 1.3-only ones; here a strict 1.2 server refuses a hello without extended_master_secret. Dual mode is tricky. The client sends one ClientHello that has to be a valid DTLS 1.2 hello and a valid DTLS 1.3 hello at the same time, and it only finds out which one it was when the server answers. If the answer is 1.2, everything from the 1.3 attempt has to disappear without a trace. Our first fallback didn't clean everything up. You can switch that bug on in the demo above. And Mallory can't force a downgrade either: a 1.3 server that gets pushed down to 1.2 writes DOWNGRD at the end of its random value, and the client notices.The record layerA DTLS 1.2 record header is 13 bytes, on every single packet. For a video call that's a lot of bytes spent on bookkeeping. DTLS 1.3 replaced it with a unified header, where the first byte is a set of flags that say what comes after it. Poke the bits:take a header apart what Mallory sees 0fix0fix1fix1E1Eepoch3Tap C, S or L to flip them.header2fflags002aseq0016length encrypted payload (22 bytes)············································ inside the lock: "hello"17 ← the real content type (application_data) now hides here, not in the header header: 5 bytesSequence number: only the low 16 bits are sent. The receiver rebuilds the full number from the ones it has seen.Epoch 3: only the low two bits (11) travel. Epoch 3 is application data. Flip the bits and watch the header shrink to 2 bytes. Then turn on “what Mallory sees” and press “next record” a few times. The encryption here is real AES, running in your browser. Three things changed.It's smaller. The smallest DTLS 1.3 header is 2 bytes. The content type (handshake, alert, application data) isn't in the header anymore, it moved inside the encryption, so Mallory can't even tell what kind of record she's looking at.The sequence number is encrypted. DTLS had to put the sequence number on every postcard, but that's also a tracking number for Mallory: she can count packets, follow a connection across networks, and measure exactly how much was sent. DTLS 1.3 encrypts those bits with a mask derived from the record's own ciphertext. Toggle "what Mallory sees" and click next a few times: the real numbers go 42, 43, 44, and she just sees noise.It's mostly implicit. Only the low 8 or 16 bits of the sequence number and the low 2 bits of the epoch are sent, and the receiver reconstructs the rest from what it expects next. That only works because the receiver keeps careful state about every epoch, which brings us to keys.Where keys come fromAs I wrote in the team's write-up: the names are scarier than the concepts. HKDF, AEAD, transcript hash, epoch, each is a small idea with a scary name.TLS 1.3 doesn't use a key, it uses a whole family of keys, each derived from the one before it and each protecting a different part of the conversation. Encrypted handshake messages get one key, application data gets another, and after a KeyUpdate you get a fresh one and the old one can be forgotten. In DTLS each of these keys lives in its own epoch, and the epoch number in the header tells the receiver which key to use.The thing that produces them is the key schedule, and it's built from one tool: HKDF, which takes some secret material and stretches it into as many independent keys as you need. You can try the actual key schedule here. It's computed in your browser:the key scheduleserver_​handshake_​traffic_​secretprotects epoch 2Derive-Secret(Handshake Secret, "s hs traffic", ClientHello..ServerHello)Encrypts the server’s EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished.value… Tap any value to see where it comes from. Every value is real HKDF with SHA-256 and the “dtls13” labels, computed in your browser. Press “new handshake” and see which values change, and which don’t. Click "new handshake" and watch every value below it change. One fresh key exchange at the top, and every key below it is new and unrelated to any previous connection. This is called forward secrecy: if someone steals the server's certificate key next year, they still can't decrypt today's call, because the keys never depended on it.The other input is the transcript hash, a running hash of every handshake message so far. Mixing it into the keys means that if Mallory changed anything, the two sides derive different keys and just can't talk. I spent a good part of June getting that transcript exactly right. Miss one byte, hash a message twice, or accidentally include a retransmission, and nothing works. And nothing tells you why it didn't :)Ciphers and post-quantum key exchangeIn July we implemented the ciphers (AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305), record number masks, seal and open. On July 1 Pion also got X25519MLKEM768, the hybrid post-quantum key exchange. It does an X25519 exchange and an ML-KEM exchange together, so the result is safe as long as either one holds up. This matters because of harvest now, decrypt later: someone recording your encrypted call today could decrypt it in fifteen years with a big enough quantum computer, unless the key exchange already resists one. By August it was on by default.Not everyone is a fan of ML-KEM, though. Daniel J. Bernstein, the person behind X25519 and ChaCha20, campaigned against an IETF draft that uses ML-KEM on its own in TLS, and says the NSA is paying to get it standardized. He calls the hybrid, the one Pion uses, "much more sensible". If ML-KEM ever falls, X25519 is still there :)Flights and ACKsReliability in DTLS 1.2 is pretty basic. Nobody acknowledges anything: if I don't hear back in time, I resend my entire flight, even if only one packet out of six was lost. And if the reply was lost instead, the other side resends its entire flight too.DTLS 1.3 added an ACK message: "here are exactly the records I got." The sender resends only the gaps, and the receiver can send an ACK as soon as it notices a hole, without waiting for a timer. Same bad luck on both sides: loss 20%DTLS 1.2no ACKs, a timer resends everythingclient hasSHEECT1CT2CVFINflight in 0.00 s0 records0.0 kB sentwaiting for you to press startDTLS 1.3ACKs say exactly what arrivedclient hasSHEECT1CT2CVFINflight in 0.00 s0 records0 ACKs0.0 kB sentwaiting for you to press start Same flight in both lanes, so only the repair differs. 50 ms each way, first timer 1 s. Records ~250 B, certificate fragments 1,200 B, ACKs ~25 B + 16 B per record number. Tap a record in flight to lose it in both lanes. Try losing just one certificate fragment, then try losing the last record, FIN. After "Finished", it really was a different story: there's a whole second state machine for session tickets and KeyUpdate, with its own ACKs and retransmissions. So getting Finished to work still leaves you with basically another protocol to implement :(Connection IDs and changing networksIn WebRTC, calls can use ICE to find a new path when the network changes (Pion has a post about that), so they don't need Connection IDs, but they matter for IoT users.Without a Connection ID, a DTLS server finds the connection a packet belongs to by where it came from: the client's IP address and port. Now walk out of your house. Your phone drops Wi-Fi, switches to cellular and gets a new address, and the server has never heard of it. Connection ID home Wi-FiWi-Fiserverphone is onWi-Fi 192.0.2.10:5000server finds the call bysource address 192.0.2.10:5000server sends video to192.0.2.10:5000video on the phonepaused · 0 frames Walk out of the house with Connection IDs off, then turn them on and try again. With a Connection ID, every record carries a short ID that the server picked, and the server finds the connection by ID instead of by address, so your connection survives the walk to the car. Pion already had CIDs for DTLS 1.2. In 1.3 they're part of the core protocol and really different, so we had to rebuild them into the new record layer, while reworking the DTLS 1.2 implementation so we wouldn't have duplicated code.Of course Mallory can make this a problem too. If the server just follows the newest address a valid record came from, she can record one real packet and resend it with the victim's address on it, and the server redirects the whole video stream at someone who never asked for it. The specs saw this coming: CIDs in both DTLS 1.2 and 1.3 already said you must check that a new address can receive before switching to it, but never said how, so many implementation didn't enforce this (including Pion's DTLS 1.2).Return Routability Check (RFC 9853) is the standard way: before trusting a new address, send it a small challenge, and only switch once the answer comes back. Try the second half of the demo with RRC off, then on.RRC has a fun backstory. While reading the IETF shepherd write-up for the RRC draft, I found this: "We have two different clients (Eclipse/Californium & Pion) that interoperate with a server." Someone had used a Pion fork for testing! I got so excited about that, I went and built a real production RRC for upstream Pion while we were still doing DTLS 1.3, instead of postponing it until after the release!Resumption, 0-RTT, and Encrypted Client HelloPre-shared keys and resumption. If the client and server talked before, or share a key from somewhere else, they can skip the certificate work entirely. Smaller handshakes, less CPU, and still forward secret when combined with a fresh key exchange.0-RTT. If you talked before, you don't have to wait at all. With a resumed session, the client can send application data in its very first flight, encrypted with keys from last time. Here's how the handshakes compare, and the catch: RTT 100 msDTLS 1.22 RTT wait · 200 msclientserver100200300 first data at 250 msDTLS 1.2 + cookie3 RTT wait · 300 msclientserver100200300 first data at 350 msDTLS 1.31 RTT wait · 100 msclientserver100200300 first data at 150 msDTLS 1.3 + 0-RTTresumed · 0 RTT waitclientserver100200300 first data at 50 ms Times are for the client's first application data to reach the server (handshake wait plus half a round trip). 1.3 adds a round trip if the server answers with HelloRetryRequest. What can Mallory do with early data? server hasn't processed anything yet Race them, then drag the RTT slider: the gaps grow with distance. Then let Mallory replay the 0-RTT early data, once as a menu request and once as a payment. Early data uses keys from an earlier session, with nothing fresh from the server, so the server can't tell a copy from the original. 0-RTT data can be replayed. There's no fresh input from the server protecting it yet, so Mallory can capture it and send it again. That's fine for "show me the menu", not fine for "pay $10", so applications have to opt in and only send things that are safe to repeat. It also gives up some forward secrecy: go back to the key schedule, turn on "with PSK" and press "new handshake" a few times. The early secret never changes, because it only comes from the PSK, so anyone who steals that PSK later can decrypt the early data.Encrypted Client Hello. TLS 1.3 already encrypts the certificate, so which site you visit is hidden, except for one field: the ClientHello carries the server's name (the SNI) in plain text, because the server needs it to pick the right certificate. ECH encrypts the real ClientHello inside an outer one that only names a generic front server:what Mallory sees in your ClientHellosecret-meeting.example, and it’s WebRTC. Noted.ClientHellolegacy_versionfe fd (claims DTLS 1.2, for old middleboxes) random… cipher_suitesTLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 supported_versionsfe fc (DTLS 1.3) supported_groupsX25519MLKEM768, X25519, secp256r1 key_shareX25519MLKEM768, 1216 bytes: … server_namesecret-meeting.example Mallory reads thisalpnwebrtc it’s a video call Switch ECH on, then flip between Mallory’s view and the server’s. The payload is really encrypted in your browser (X25519 and AES-GCM standing in for HPKE), and the server’s view is really decrypted from it. While implementing ECH, I wanted our implementation to match crypto/tls, because I felt it was the right thing to do. But as soon as I started, I found two places where Go's own crypto/tls was too lenient with ECH configurations, and sent them patches (one, two). So we went back to doing it our own way, which turned out to be the stricter implementation.Testing the implementationI think setting up interop tests was the best decision we made all year. Testing Pion against itself only proves both sides share the same assumptions, so in April I created pion/dtls-interop and froze releases from main until interop was ready. It tests Pion against:OpenSSL 3 and 4BoringSSLwolfSSLMbed TLSthe TLS-Anvil conformance suitePion's own v3On September 28, when DTLS 1.3 went into Pion WebRTC's next major version, I added it to pion/browser-tests, which runs Pion WebRTC against Chrome, Firefox, Edge and Safari.The report before releaseAnthropic's OSS scanner went through pion/dtls and sent us a report. On October 16 I opened #1228, "Fix all issues reported by anthropics/oss-scanner", and spent the busiest two weeks of the whole project working through it. Most of the real issues were in DTLS 1.2, session resumption and shared code that had been in production for years, not the new DTLS 1.3 code, and we fixed them on both main and the v3 branch so existing users can upgrade without changing anything. After spending so much time anxious about breaking stuff, that felt really good :)sirzooro independently reported a few of the same issues (and others), found with Claude Opus 5.5.Why exporting connection state is trickyThere was one finding we couldn't fix in code.Pion v3 lets you export a connection's state and resume it later, for example to hand a connection from one process to another. The scanner pointed out that nothing stops both the original and the restored connection from continuing to send. Both would keep encrypting with the same AES-GCM key and the same sequence numbers, and the nonce is built from the sequence number.Reusing a nonce with AES-GCM is one of the worst things you can do in cryptography. Here's why: guess use a fresh nonce for each message connection A sendsconnection B sends same key, nonce A: same key, nonce B: (reused!)✗ C1⊕C2 has nothing to do with P1⊕P2. It’s noise.guess ⊕ (C1⊕C2) at 0:“”Slide the guess until the other line reads. Slide Mallory’s guess along until the “reveals” row turns into words. Then tick “fresh nonce” and try again. AES-GCM encrypts by XORing your message with a keystream generated from the key and the nonce. Same key and nonce means same keystream, so XORing the two ciphertexts cancels the keystream out and leaves the two plaintexts XORed together. Mallory doesn't need the key: she guesses a likely word in one message, and the other message shows up around it. The same reuse also leaks enough for her to forge tags.Sadly we couldn't make the v3 API safe without breaking everyone who uses it, so v3 now documents loudly that a restored state must be used exactly once. In v4, Resume requires ExportState, which closes the original connection as part of the export, so there's no way to keep using both.Thank youI'm really happy with what we built. I never thought I'd lead a project this big all the way to the end, and that still feels a bit weird. But the part I'm most proud of is the people. Whenever I got stuck, or talked about a problem for hours in our Discord server or group chats, someone was always there to listen and help.None of this would exist without the people I built it with: Sean DuBois, Theodor Signebøen Midtlien, Adriano Sela Aviles, R Chiu, Jade Kolos, Júlia Borges Paschoalinoto, Julia-Elena Roman and Jan Muška. Thank you for all the reviews and testing, and sorry for how annoying I was about stuff I found cool :)Huge thanks to Thomas Legris. He runs DTLS for a very large fleet of IoT devices with Pion on the server side, and at that scale every allocation per connection gets multiplied by hundreds of thousands. One of his PRs starts with "At scale (700k connections) - I detected some heavy allocations, especially at handshake." Over the year he sent a lot of optimizations:fewer copies and allocations in the handshakepre-allocated buffers for marshallingpooled timersa reworked PacketConn with fewer goroutines per connection, in pion/dtls and pion/transporta fix for a connection leakThen he ran the release candidates in production, and they worked without a single problem.Resumption got tested before it was even tagged, and I can't tell you how happy that made me :) ybaldus opened an issue about deadlines while building SWIM on pion/dtls, which "requires short lived connections and session resumption to be scalable." When I said resumption wasn't tagged yet: "Don't mind tagging it yet I can also use the current master commit." The report turned into a fix that applies read and write deadlines to the handshake.Leonard (ltlobaro) did the same from the IoT side, where "DTLS 1.2 handshakes easily take up most of the device traffic". They played with the DTLS 1.3 resumption example, found that key logging didn't work with DTLS 1.3, and it was fixed in rc.5 the same day.devArnoud ran DTLS 1.3 against a cellular modem whose TLS stack is wolfSSL baked into its firmware, and every handshake failed. When the server asked the modem to send its ClientHello again, wolfSSL sent the same extensions in a different order. The spec doesn't strictly allow that, but for compatibility Pion accepts it now.enobufs tried DTLS 1.3 with WebRTC early and helped with the keying-material exporter.Thanks to Philipp Hancke for testing DTLS 1.3 in his SPED implementation, which embeds the DTLS handshake in STUN, and for noticing that Pion sent a session ticket even to clients that never use resumption.Thank you to everyone who reviewed, tested, reported and fixed things along the way. Thanks to NLnet and the NGI0 Commons Fund for funding work like this, and to the Anthropic OSS scanner team for the report that made v4 safer before anyone found out the hard way.And thank you for reading this far :) Now go break something.Come chat with us on the Pion Discord about anything.P.S. Everything went perfectly except one silly mistake: I forgot to wire the message hooks into DTLS 1.3 after refactoring the handshake messages, and one hook was left taking a 1.2-only type, so we had to break the API in v4.0.1, our very first patch a few minutes later after we tagged v4 :(
